Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' These items describe opposing levels of verbal access to the trauma memory and are hard to reconcile as the same patient's current self-report.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked memory disturbance items ('some moments are extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'there are parts of the event I simply cannot remember'). Although fragmented trauma memory can coexist with disclosure, the wording 'very easily' is hard to reconcile with this level of fragmentation in the same profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
issues.explanation: Across Memory and Negative Appraisals, reporting that one can talk about the event 'very easily' sits in tension with the appraisal 'If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it.' Patients may force themselves to discuss trauma despite distress, but these two statements point in opposite directions and are difficult to integrate clinically without additional context.

vignette:
At 63, Tane had spent most of his adult life in other people's emergencies. As a community organizer, he was used to tense public meetings, calls from frightened tenants, arguments in church basements and school auditoriums, and the steady work of helping neighborhoods respond when systems failed them. He was divorced, lived alone, and had long taken pride in being the person who stayed calm when everyone else was upset. The accident that now divided his life into before and after happened on an ordinary workday while he was driving between meetings. Traffic had slowed near an intersection where police vehicles had already gathered around an earlier incident. He remembered the blue uniforms at the roadside, the jerking line of cars, and someone behind him leaning on a horn. Then came a burst of shouting from outside his driver's side window-angry voices he could not place now, only the sharp force of them-and the violent impact of another vehicle hitting his car hard enough to spin it.

What remained with him from that day came in broken pieces rather than a full story. Some fragments were painfully exact: the sight of a police officer running toward the wreck, the metallic smell inside the car, a sudden pressure in his chest as he struggled to breathe, his hands shaking uncontrollably while someone yelled for him not to move. Other stretches were simply gone. He knew there had been people pulling at the door, questions being asked, and later a sequence of medical checks and phone calls, but there were parts he could not retrieve no matter how hard he tried. In the first sessions he would stop midsentence and press his fingers together as if trying to hold onto language. He would say he knew what happened, that it was there somewhere, but when he tried to describe it the words just would not come. This inability to tell it straight unsettled him almost as much as the crash itself.

In the months afterward, his world became dotted with moments that made no sense to people around him but felt immediately dangerous to him. At organizing meetings, if a resident raised their voice in frustration-even in the measured, controlled way people do when they are trying to be heard-Tane's body reacted before he could think. His shoulders tightened, his heart began pounding, and he felt the same internal jolt he had felt in the car when angry voices flared nearby. He could tell himself he was in a recreation center or nonprofit office, not trapped behind a steering wheel, but his body did not seem to believe him. He had come to see his own physical reactions as an enemy presence, something disloyal inside him that kept dragging him back toward danger even when he was objectively safe.

Police uniforms were especially hard. His work regularly brought him into contact with city officials, security staff, and officers stationed outside public events. The dark uniforms, badges, and heavy belts could pull him abruptly into the clearest surviving shard of the accident scene: the officer moving toward his window while he sat disoriented and pinned in place. On those days he found reasons to remain at the back of the room, to let younger colleagues handle check-ins, permits, or conversations that involved uniformed personnel. He did not explain much. He simply said he was tired or not feeling up to it. Over time, others noticed that he was less present at the meetings where confrontation was most likely. A colleague took over several neighborhood forums because Tane had begun leaving early after arguments broke out, and he felt ashamed watching his role shrink in the work that had once defined him.

He also carried a hard private conviction about the crash. He believed it happened because of the way he had acted, though when he tried to explain exactly what he should have done differently-driven another route, reacted faster, not gone out that day-his reasoning circled without relief. What stayed firm was the conclusion that he had failed in some essential way. That belief sat alongside a deadened emotional state that frightened him for different reasons. Friends from church and longtime organizers checked on him, but he often felt as if he were answering from a great distance. He could describe what others expected him to feel more easily than he could feel it. He said he was "fine," then sat alone afterward sensing almost nothing, disturbed by how empty he had become.

He finally sought help after a public meeting on neighborhood safety. A disagreement in the room escalated only mildly, but one man's angry tone froze him where he sat. When he turned, he saw two officers at the back wall, and his mind filled with the same unwanted images of the wrecked car and the officer at his window. He left before the meeting ended and sat in his car for nearly an hour, unable to steady himself enough to drive. What frightened him most was not only that the memories still broke through, but that he no longer trusted his own body or his own account of what had happened. He came in hoping, cautiously, that he might find words for the blank and broken parts of that day, and afraid that if he did not, the life he had built around being dependable and present would continue to narrow around him.
